messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

As a renowned film director, Thomas had always been drawn to the thrill of capturing life's most intense moments on camera. But it was during a shoot in an abandoned warehouse that his own life took a drastic turn. A sudden collapse of the structure left him trapped under the rubble, fighting for air and consciousness. The memories of those harrowing minutes are forever seared into his mind like vivid frames of a film he can't shake. In the aftermath, Thomas began to question his own adequacy as a director and, more fundamentally, as a person. He couldn't help but wonder why this had happened to him – was it some cosmic punishment for pushing the limits too far? These ruminations on inadequacy soon spilled over into other areas of his life. He started feeling like he was losing himself, becoming someone unrecognizable even to those closest to him, including his partner. As these negative self-appraisals took hold, Thomas found himself employing various maladaptive strategies to cope with the anxiety that now gripped him. He avoided dark places or enclosed spaces, instinctively associating them with the suffocating sensation he experienced during the accident. He also became a master of distraction, filling every spare moment with work or meaningless activities to avoid confronting his thoughts and memories. But these avoidance tactics only seemed to heighten Thomas's sense of threat. The world began to feel like a minefield of potential dangers – loud noises made him jump, and he found himself perpetually on edge, scanning for signs of impending doom. Even the creaks and groans of the old film sets where he worked now sent his heart racing. Memories of that fateful day lingered, refusing to be silenced. Thomas would see flashes of debris falling, hear the sound of crumbling concrete – it was as if the event had become an indelible part of him. He struggled to verbalize these memories; they remained stubbornly nonverbal, manifesting instead in a perpetual sense of unease that colored every waking moment. These fragmented recollections not only contributed to his threat appraisal but also reinforced Thomas's negative self-perceptions. Why couldn't he shake off the feeling of being an inadequate person? The accident had happened on his watch; it was a stark reminder that, no matter how much control he exerted over his film sets, life itself remained unpredictably cruel. In turn, these intensified feelings of inadequacy led Thomas to rely even more heavily on maladaptive strategies – more distraction, more avoidance. It became a self-reinforcing cycle where his inability to confront the past fed into an ever-present sense of danger, which in turn drove him further away from confronting those very memories. Despite this vicious loop, it was only when Thomas found himself at odds with his long-time partner over his increasing withdrawal that he realized he needed help. The fear of losing not just himself but also the people he loved most finally brought him to seek therapy – a move he hoped would be the first step towards reclaiming his life and breaking free from the suffocating grip of his memories.
